Part I
Getting Started
Chapter 1

Welcome to DRAWmaster

DRAWmaster is a vector drawing program: a tool for building pictures out of shapes, lines and paths that stay perfectly sharp at any size. It belongs to the just a… family of apps and works in the tradition of Serif's DrawPlus — the same ideas, the same way of drawing.

What vector drawing is

There are two kinds of picture on a computer. A bitmap (or raster) image — a photograph, or anything you paint in PAINTcanvas — is a grid of coloured dots; blow it up and the dots show as fuzzy squares. A vector image is different: it is stored as instructions — “a red star here, a blue line there” — so the computer re-draws it crisply at whatever size you ask. Zoom in a hundred times and the edges stay razor-sharp.

That makes vector drawing the right tool for logos, icons, diagrams, maps, badges and illustrations — anything that must look clean at any size, from a business-card corner to a banner across a wall.

The object model

Everything you draw in DRAWmaster is an object, and there are only a handful of kinds:

  • Rectangles and ellipses — the two basic boxed shapes;
  • QuickShapes — ready-made outlines such as stars, arrows, hearts and speech bubbles;
  • Lines — a single straight segment;
  • Freehand paths — a flowing line you draw by hand, as if with a pencil;
  • Pen polylines — a shape built point by point, which you can leave open or close into a filled outline;
  • Text — artistic text that behaves like a shape (fill, outline, gradient and effects all apply), and can be flowed along a path;
  • Images — a bitmap picture placed on the canvas, embedded in the drawing;
  • Dimension lines and connectors — technical-drawing objects: a measured line with a length label, and a link between two objects that follows them as they move.

Because they are all objects, the skills are shared: whatever the kind, you select it, move it, give it a fill and an outline, and lift it off the page with a shadow or glow — all in exactly the same way. Learn those moves once and they apply to everything you draw.

The just a… family

DRAWmaster has three companions, and they are built to work together:

  • PAINTcanvas is the raster image editor — DRAWmaster can hand a finished drawing across to it for photo-style touch-ups;
  • PAGEdesigner lays out printed pages — posters, flyers, newsletters;
  • WEBcreator builds websites the same way.

They share the CREATORsuite launcher and a common Documents/just a… folder, so your work is always easy to find. Once you know one app, the others feel familiar.

About this guide

This User Guide is the complete reference. It is organised in parts: the first gets you working, the middle teaches each skill in depth with step-by-step procedures, then come worked projects you can follow start to finish, output and sharing, and finally a reference section — menus, shortcuts, a catalogue of every QuickShape, and a glossary.

NoteThroughout, a numbered “To …” box is a procedure you can follow exactly. A Tip suggests a faster or better way. A Remember box flags something easy to forget.

For a gentler first read, start with the Quick Start Guide (Help ▸ Quick Start Guide), which takes you from a blank canvas to a finished drawing in a dozen short steps.

Conventions used here

A few conventions keep the instructions short:

  • Menu ▸ Command means “open this menu and choose this command”, e.g. File ▸ Save as SVG….
  • Keys are shown like Ctrl+S; on a Mac read Ctrl as Cmd.
  • Click means the left mouse button; drag means press, move, release; double-click finishes a pen shape.
Chapter 2

Starting Out

This chapter covers the very first things: launching the program, the canvas you draw on, and starting a new drawing at the size you want.

Launching the program

Open just a… DRAWmaster from the CREATORsuite launcher, from your system's application menu, or by running draw in a terminal. It opens straight onto a blank white canvas, ready to draw.

Starting a new drawing

DRAWmaster opens with a default canvas, but you can start fresh at a chosen size at any time.

To start a new drawing

  1. Choose File ▸ New… (Ctrl+N).
  2. Pick a canvas size from the list — a general 1000 × 700, an A4 page (794 × 1123), full-HD 1920 × 1080, or a square 800 × 800.
  3. Click Create. The canvas clears to the new size, ready for your first shape.
NoteThe canvas size sets the drawing’s coordinate space and the proportions of an exported PNG. Because the drawing is vector, you can still scale the result up or down afterwards without losing sharpness.

Saving and opening

DRAWmaster saves your work as an SVG file — the standard vector format, readable by browsers, other drawing programs and the web.

To save your drawing

  1. Choose File ▸ Save as SVG… (Ctrl+S).
  2. Give it a name. It is saved into your shared Documents/just a… folder by default, so the launcher can find it.
  3. DRAWmaster quietly tucks the full, editable drawing inside the SVG, so it can re-open its own files with every shape intact.

To open a drawing

  1. Choose File ▸ Open SVG… (Ctrl+O) and pick an .svg file.
  2. A drawing DRAWmaster saved itself opens fully editable.
RememberDRAWmaster can re-open the SVGs it saved with every object editable, because it stores its object list inside the file. A plain SVG made by another program still displays as a picture elsewhere, but DRAWmaster cannot break it back into editable shapes.
Chapter 3

The Workspace

Everything you do happens in the workspace: your canvas in the middle, the drawing tools down the left, the style controls across the top, and a status bar below. This chapter names every part so the rest of the guide can refer to them.

A tour of the window

A new drawing opens with the white canvas centred on a grey pasteboard and everything you need arranged around it.

The parts are:

  • the menu bar across the top — File, Edit and Help;
  • the Style toolbar below it — fill, line, width, QuickShape, effects and zoom;
  • the vertical tool palette down the left edge;
  • the canvas itself in the centre;
  • the status bar along the bottom, which shows the pointer's position.

The tool palette

The vertical tool palette on the left holds the tools you draw and edit with. Click one to select it; it stays active until you choose another.

From the top, the tools are the Select pointer, the Node tool (for reshaping curves), Freehand (a pencil), the Pen (for Bézier curves), Line, Rectangle, Ellipse, QuickShape, Text, Image, the Dimension line (a measured line with end ticks and an automatic length label) and the Connector (a line that links two objects and stays attached as they move). Each is covered in detail in Part II.

TipChoosing the Select tool is the quickest way to stop drawing and go back to picking things up and moving them.

The Style toolbar

The horizontal Style toolbar along the top sets how the next shape will look — and restyles the selected one.

  • Fill — the colour inside a shape (the button shows the current colour);
  • Line — the colour of the outline;
  • Width — the outline thickness, in pixels (0 for no outline);
  • Shape — which QuickShape the QuickShape tool draws;
  • Effects… — the drop shadow and glow for the selected object;
  • Zoom — zoom in, zoom out, and back to 100%.

Moving around and zooming

You will zoom in to place things precisely and out to judge the whole drawing.

To change the zoom

  1. Click Zoom + or Zoom − on the Style toolbar to step in or out, or
  2. click 100% to return to actual size.

When the drawing is larger than the window, scroll bars appear around the canvas so you can slide to any part of it. The status bar at the bottom shows the pointer's exact position in canvas coordinates — useful for lining a shape up precisely.

Part II
Core Skills
Chapter 4

Drawing Shapes

Rectangles, ellipses and QuickShapes are the building blocks of most drawings. This chapter covers drawing each of them, and the two dozen ready-made QuickShapes.

Rectangles and ellipses

To draw a rectangle or an ellipse

  1. Choose the Rectangle or Ellipse tool from the tool palette.
  2. Press on the canvas where one corner should be, drag to the opposite corner, and release.
  3. The shape appears with the current fill and outline, and is left selected so you can adjust it at once.

Each new shape takes the Fill and Line colours and the Width currently shown on the Style toolbar — so set those first if you know the look you want, or change them afterwards with the shape selected.

QuickShapes

QuickShapes are ready-made outlines — you do not draw their edges by hand, you simply drag out a box and the shape fills it. DRAWmaster has 18 of them.

To draw a QuickShape

  1. On the Style toolbar, pick a shape from the Shape list (choosing one switches to the QuickShape tool automatically).
  2. Drag a box on the canvas; the shape is drawn to fit it.
  3. Resize, recolour or move it afterwards like any other object.

They cover geometry (triangle, right triangle, diamond, pentagon, hexagon, octagon, parallelogram, trapezoid), stars (five- and six-point), arrows (single, double and a chevron), a cross, and the expressive shapes — heart, lightning bolt, speech bubble and cloud — ready for a badge, a diagram or a caption.

The QuickShape catalogue

For reference, here is every QuickShape by name, in the order they appear in the Shape list:

QuickShape
Triangle
Right triangle
Diamond
Pentagon
Hexagon
Octagon
Star (5-point)
Star (6-point)
Arrow

TipA speech bubble makes an instant caption; a star or a seal draws the eye to the one thing that matters; arrows and a chevron turn a set of boxes into a diagram or a flow chart.
Chapter 5

Drawing Lines and Paths

Where shapes give a drawing its solid forms, lines and paths give it movement and detail — a rule, a connector, a flowing hand-drawn stroke, or a custom outline you build point by point.

Straight lines

To draw a straight line

  1. Choose the Line tool.
  2. Press where the line should start, drag to where it should end, and release.
  3. A line has no fill — only a colour and a width, both set on the Style toolbar.

A line is the simplest object there is: two points, a colour and a thickness. Set the Width high for a bold rule, or to 1 for a hairline.

Freehand drawing

The Freehand tool is a pencil: it records your pointer's path as you drag, giving a natural, hand-drawn stroke.

To draw a freehand stroke

  1. Choose the Freehand tool.
  2. Press and hold, then draw — the line follows your pointer exactly.
  3. Release to finish. The stroke becomes a path object you can recolour, re-weight, move or delete.
TipFreehand is ideal for signatures, sketchy underlines, loose doodles and the organic lines that a perfectly straight tool cannot give you. Zoom in first for finer control.

The Pen: point-by-point polylines

The Pen tool builds a shape one corner at a time — the precise way to draw an exact outline, a polygon, a zig-zag or a many-sided star of your own.

To draw with the Pen

  1. Choose the Pen tool.
  2. Click once for each corner; a line follows your pointer so you can see the next segment before you place it.
  3. To finish as a closed, filled shape, double-click — the outline joins up and fills with the current fill colour.
  4. To finish as an open line instead, press Enter — the points stay joined but the shape is not closed and not filled.
NoteA closed pen shape behaves like any other filled object — it takes a fill, an outline and effects. An open pen line behaves like a multi-segment line. Choose which you want by how you finish: double-click to close, Enter to leave open.
Chapter 6

Editing Nodes and Curves

Straight segments only take a drawing so far. The Pen tool draws true Bézier curves, and the Node tool reshapes any path by dragging its nodes and control handles — the heart of precise vector drawing. Any shape can be turned into an editable curve with Convert to Curves.

Drawing curves with the Pen

The Pen tool lays down a path one node at a time. How you place each node decides the shape of the curve that flows through it:

To draw a Bézier curve

  1. Choose the Pen tool.
  2. Click to drop a corner node — the path turns sharply through it.
  3. Click and drag to drop a smooth node — dragging pulls out a pair of control handles, and the path curves gracefully through the node.
  4. Carry on clicking and dragging to build the path; a live preview follows your pointer.
  5. Double-click to finish as a closed, filled shape, or press Enter to finish as an open curve.
NoteA curve drawn this way is stored as real cubic Bézier segments and exported as an SVG <path d="M… C…">, so it stays perfectly smooth at any size and in any browser.

Reshaping with the Node tool

The Node tool (second in the palette) edits an existing path. Click a node path to show its nodes as little squares and its control handles as small circles on stalks.

To reshape a path

  1. Choose the Node tool and click the path you want to edit.
  2. Drag a node (a square) to move that point of the path.
  3. Drag a control handle (a circle) to change how the curve bends into and out of the node — a smooth node keeps its two handles mirrored, for an unbroken curve.
TipA smooth node gives a graceful, continuous curve; a corner node gives a sharp change of direction. Mix the two along one path for shapes that are part curved, part angular.

Convert to Curves

Any ordinary object — a rectangle, an ellipse, a QuickShape, a line or a pen shape — can be turned into an editable node path, so you can push its outline about freely.

To convert a shape to curves

  1. Select the object with the Select tool.
  2. Choose Edit ▸ Convert to Curves (Ctrl+Shift+C).
  3. The shape becomes a node path and the Node tool switches on, ready for you to reshape it.
NoteConverting an ellipse gives four smooth nodes with Bézier handles — the mathematically exact curve — so you can pull a circle into an egg, a leaf or a teardrop. Converting a rectangle or a QuickShape gives corner nodes you can round off or drag into a new outline.
Chapter 7

Placing Pictures

A vector drawing can hold photographs and bitmaps too. The Image tool brings a picture onto the canvas as an object you can move, resize, rotate and layer like any other — ideal for a logo photo, a texture, or a scan to trace over.

Importing an image

To place a picture on the canvas

  1. Choose the Image tool (the picture icon at the foot of the tool palette) and click on the canvas — or choose File ▸ Import Image….
  2. Pick a PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP or WebP file.
  3. The picture appears, scaled to fit the canvas and left selected, ready to position.

Because an image is an object, you move it, resize it by dragging its handles, rotate it, put it on a layer, and stack it in front of or behind your shapes.

How images are stored

When you import a picture, DRAWmaster embeds it inside the drawing — the file's data travels with the SVG as a self-contained data URI. That means a saved drawing is a single file you can move or share without losing its pictures.

NoteAn image is written into the exported SVG as a real <image> element with its embedded data, so the drawing opens complete in a browser or another program — nothing to link, nothing to lose.
TipPlace a photo or a scanned sketch on a lower layer, drop its opacity, and draw over the top with the Pen and shapes — a quick way to trace a picture into clean vector artwork.
Chapter 8

Working with Text

The Text tool adds artistic text — words that are a drawing object in their own right, so they take a fill, an outline, a gradient and effects exactly like a shape, and stay perfectly sharp at any size.

Adding text

To add a line of text

  1. Choose the Text tool (the T at the foot of the tool palette).
  2. Click on the canvas where the text should begin.
  3. In the dialog, type your text, choose a font — every font bundled with the suite is offered, alongside your system fonts — and set a pixel size.
  4. Click OK. The text appears in the current fill colour and is left selected.

Because text is a true object, you move it, recolour it, outline it and give it a shadow or glow just as you would a shape — and it is exported as real, selectable <text> in the SVG, so it stays crisp and searchable on the web.

Editing and styling text

To change the words, font or size

  1. Select the text object with the Select tool.
  2. Choose Edit ▸ Edit Text….
  3. Change the text, font or size, and click OK.

Set the Fill for the colour of the letters and, if you want an outlined look, give it a Line colour and a Width. A gradient fill and the shadow/glow Effects both apply to text too.

TipOutline-only text — no fill, a bold line colour and a wide width — gives a clean “stencil” headline; a gradient fill gives a bright, modern title.

Fitting text to a path

Text need not run in a straight line. Fit Text to Path attaches a line of artistic text to a line, a freehand or pen path, or a Bézier curve, so the letters flow along it — for a curved headline, a badge rim, a ribbon or a wave.

To flow text along a path

  1. Draw the path the text should follow — a line, a freehand or pen stroke, or a Bézier curve (and convert a shape to curves first if you want to run text round it).
  2. Add a line of Text as usual.
  3. With the Select tool, select both the text and the path (click one, then Shift-click the other).
  4. Choose Text ▸ Fit Text to Path. The glyphs lay themselves along the path, each turned to follow its direction.

The text keeps its fill, outline and font; change the words with Edit Text and they re-flow along the same path. To straighten it out again, choose Text ▸ Detach Text from Path.

NoteText on a path is written into the exported SVG as a real <textPath> following a path definition, so the curved text renders — and stays selectable — in a web browser.
TipFlow text around a circle you have converted to curves for a classic round “seal” or stamp; flow it along a gentle wave for a lively banner headline.
Chapter 9

Selecting and Moving Objects

Once something is on the canvas you will want to pick it up, move it, and get rid of mistakes. Those moves all start with the Select tool.

Selecting an object

To select an object

  1. Choose the Select tool (the pointer at the top of the palette).
  2. Click an object. A dashed blue box appears around it to show it is selected.
  3. Click a different object to select that one instead, or click empty canvas to deselect.
NoteClicking picks the topmost object under the pointer — the one drawn most recently. To reach something behind it, move the object on top out of the way first.

Moving an object

With the Select tool, press on a selected object and drag it to a new place; release to drop it. The whole object moves together, keeping its size, colour and any effects. The status bar shows the pointer's position as you go, so you can line something up against a coordinate.

Deleting an object

To delete an object

  1. Select it with the Select tool.
  2. Press Delete (or Backspace). The object is removed.
  3. Changed your mind? Edit ▸ Undo (Ctrl+Z) brings it straight back.
Chapter 10

Transforming Objects

Selecting an object does more than let you move it. With the Select tool a selected object shows a frame of handles — eight around the edge to resize it, and one above to spin it round. Resizing and rotating are the two transforms every object can take.

The selection handles

Click an object with the Select tool and a blue frame appears, studded with handles: a small square at each corner and at the middle of each edge, and a round rotate handle on a short stalk above the top edge.

The frame (and every handle) turns with the object, so once something is rotated its handles still line up with its own edges — resizing stays intuitive however far it has been spun.

Resizing an object

To resize an object

  1. Select it with the Select tool.
  2. Drag a corner handle to resize both ways at once, or an edge handle to stretch along one axis only.
  3. Hold Shift while dragging a corner to resize proportionally, keeping the original shape’s aspect ratio.
  4. Release when it is the size you want.
NoteResizing text scales its point size rather than squashing the letters, so type stays properly proportioned. A line or path scales by stretching the gaps between its points.

Rotating an object

To rotate an object

  1. Select it, then drag the round rotate handle on the stalk above the top edge.
  2. The object turns about its centre as you drag; the status bar and frame follow it round.
  3. Hold Shift to snap the angle to convenient 15° steps.

Rotation is stored with the object as an angle, so it survives a save and re-open, and it is written into the exported SVG as a real transform — a shape rotates with a transform matrix, a piece of text with an explicit rotate() — so it renders identically on screen, in a PNG and in any web browser.

TipRotation and resize combine freely: stretch a shape to the proportions you want first, then spin it to the angle you need. Undo (Ctrl+Z) steps back through each transform.

Flipping (mirroring)

Flipping mirrors an object — turning it into its own reflection. It is the quick way to make a left-facing shape face right, or to build a symmetrical pair.

To flip an object

  1. Select one or more objects with the Select tool.
  2. Choose Arrange ▸ Flip Horizontal to mirror left-to-right,
  3. or Arrange ▸ Flip Vertical to mirror top-to-bottom.
NoteFlipping mirrors the whole selection about its combined centre, so flipping several objects together keeps their arrangement and mirrors it as one.
Chapter 11

Duplicating, Cloning and Locking

Three housekeeping commands make a busy drawing easier to manage: Duplicate makes an instant copy, and Lock pins an object down so you cannot select or move it by accident.

Duplicating an object

Duplicate (sometimes called clone) makes an exact copy of the selection, offset a little so you can see it — the fastest way to build a row of identical buttons, a scatter of stars, or a repeated motif.

To duplicate the selection

  1. Select one or more objects with the Select tool.
  2. Choose Edit ▸ Duplicate (Ctrl+D).
  3. A copy appears, nudged down and to the right, and is left selected — drag it into place, or duplicate again for a cascade.
NoteA duplicate is a fully independent object — recolour or reshape it without touching the original. Duplicating a group copies the whole group as a new, separate group.

Locking and unlocking

Locking an object pins it to the canvas: a locked object cannot be clicked, selected, dragged or rubber-band-picked, so it stays put while you work on everything around it. It is ideal for a background, a template or a traced reference you want to draw over without nudging.

To lock and unlock

  1. Select the object (or objects) you want to protect.
  2. Choose Arrange ▸ Lock / Unlock (Ctrl+L). The object is now locked and cannot be selected by clicking.
  3. To work on it again, it is still listed — select it through its layer, or choose Lock / Unlock again while it is selected to release it.
RememberBecause a locked object ignores clicks, the quickest way to reach it again is to put it on its own layer (see “Layers”), so you can always find and unlock it.
Chapter 12

Fill, Line and Width

Every shape in DRAWmaster has two coats of colour — a fill inside and an outline around — plus an outline width. Those three controls, all on the Style toolbar, carry most of a drawing's style.

Setting the fill colour

To set a fill colour

  1. Click the Fill button on the Style toolbar.
  2. Pick a colour in the colour dialog — drag in the wheel, type a hex value, or set the alpha (opacity) slider for a see-through fill.
  3. Click OK. If an object is selected, its fill changes at once; otherwise the colour waits for the next shape you draw.
NoteThe Fill button is tinted with the current fill colour, so you can always see what the next shape will be filled with.

Setting the line colour

To set a line (outline) colour

  1. Click the Line button on the Style toolbar.
  2. Pick a colour and click OK.

The outline sits around the edge of a shape (or is the whole of a line or an open pen path). A dark, thin outline makes a shape crisp; a thick, contrasting one makes it bold.

Setting the outline width

The Width spin box on the Style toolbar sets the outline thickness in pixels.

To change the outline width

  1. Select the object (or set the width before drawing).
  2. Type a number in the Width box, or click its up/down arrows.
  3. A width of 0 removes the outline entirely — useful for a shape that should be a pure block of colour.
TipA shape with a bold fill and no outline (width 0) reads as a clean, modern block; a shape with no fill and a thick outline reads as a frame or a ring. The three ways — fill only, outline only, both — are shown together below.
Chapter 13

Gradient and Texture Fills

Instead of a single flat colour, a shape can be filled with a gradient — a smooth blend between two colours — or with a texture: a tiled or stretched image. DRAWmaster offers a linear and a radial gradient, and a texture / pattern fill drawn from an image file or your local texture library.

Applying a gradient

To fill a shape with a gradient

  1. Select the shape with the Select tool — a rectangle, ellipse, QuickShape, a closed pen shape, or even a piece of text.
  2. Click Gradient… on the Style toolbar (or Edit ▸ Gradient Fill…).
  3. Choose Linear or Radial, pick the start and end colours, and for a linear gradient set the angle.
  4. Click OK. The gradient fills the shape, mapped across its bounding box.

A gradient is exported as a real SVG <linearGradient> or <radialGradient>, so it renders identically on screen, in an exported PNG, and in any web browser — and it survives a save-and-reopen with its colours and angle intact.

Removing a gradient

To go back to a flat fill, open Gradient… again and click Remove gradient — or simply click the Fill button and pick a solid colour, which replaces the gradient.

TipA radial gradient from a pale centre to a deep edge gives a shape a soft, rounded, “lit” look; a linear gradient at a shallow angle makes a clean modern background bar.

Texture and pattern fills

A shape can also be filled with a texture — an image painted inside its outline. DRAWmaster can tile the image (repeating it at its natural size) or stretch one copy to fill the shape's box, and it can draw the picture from a file you choose or from your local texture library — a set of categorised textures (wood, marble, brick, metal, paper, foliage and more) stored on your machine.

To fill a shape with a texture

  1. Select a shape with the Select tool — a rectangle, ellipse, QuickShape or a closed pen shape.
  2. Choose Edit ▸ Texture / Pattern Fill….
  3. Either pick a library category and a texture from it, or click Browse for an image file… to use your own picture.
  4. Choose a fill mode — Tile to repeat the image, or Stretch to fit to scale one copy across the shape.
  5. Click OK. The texture fills the shape.

The chosen image is embedded in the drawing as a self-contained data URI, exactly like a placed picture — so a texture-filled shape travels with the file and survives a save-and-reopen. In the exported SVG the texture becomes a real <pattern> with an embedded <image>, so it renders in any browser.

NoteThe texture library is read live from ~/.local/share/justapps/textures if it is present on your machine; DRAWmaster never copies it into itself. If the folder is absent the dialog simply offers the Browse for an image file… route instead.
TipA texture fill replaces a gradient (and vice versa). To go back to a flat colour, open the dialog and click Remove texture, or pick a solid Fill colour.
Chapter 14

Opacity, Dashes, Arrowheads and Combining Shapes

A handful of finishing controls give a drawing polish: making an object see-through, styling a line as dashed or dotted or tipping it with an arrowhead, and welding several shapes into one with the Combine commands.

Object opacity

Every object can be made partly transparent, so whatever lies behind it shows through — useful for soft overlays, tints and layered washes of colour.

To set an object’s opacity

  1. Select the object with the Select tool.
  2. Choose Edit ▸ Opacity… and set a value from 0 (invisible) to 100 (solid).
  3. Click OK.
NoteOpacity is saved with the object and written into the exported SVG as an opacity value, so it renders the same on screen, in a PNG and in a browser.

Dashed and dotted lines

A line, a freehand or pen path, or a node path can be drawn solid, dashed or dotted — and tipped with an arrowhead at one or both ends, for connectors, pointers and diagrams.

To style a line’s dashes and arrowheads

  1. Select a line, a path or a node path.
  2. Choose Edit ▸ Line Style (Dashes & Arrows)….
  3. Pick a dash style — solid, dashed or dotted — and an arrowhead option — none, start, end or both ends.
  4. Click OK.

The dash pattern scales with the line's width, and an arrowhead is drawn in the line's own colour — both are written into the exported SVG, so a dashed arrow looks the same everywhere.

Combining shapes

The Combine commands weld two or more overlapping shapes into a single editable outline, using the three classic boolean operations.

To combine shapes

  1. Select two or more overlapping shapes.
  2. Choose Arrange ▸ Combine ▸ Union to merge them into one outline,
  3. Subtract to cut the upper shapes out of the lowest one,
  4. or Intersect to keep only the area they all share.
NoteThe result is a single node path, so you can keep reshaping it with the Node tool, give it a gradient or an effect, or combine it again. It is the quick way to build a custom shape no single QuickShape provides.
Chapter 15

Dimension Lines and Connectors

Two tools serve technical drawing — plans, diagrams and flow charts. A dimension line draws a measured line with end ticks and an automatic length label; a connector joins two objects with a line that stays attached as they move.

Drawing a dimension line

A dimension line is the annotation you see on a plan: a line spanning a distance, capped with a short tick at each end, and labelled with the length it measures. DRAWmaster works the length out for you and keeps the label upright.

To draw a dimension line

  1. Choose the Dimension line tool from the tool palette.
  2. Press where the measurement should start, drag to where it should end, and release.
  3. The line appears with end ticks and a length label showing the distance in the current measurement unit.
NoteThe label reads out in whatever unit is set in View ▸ Measurement Units — pixels, millimetres or centimetres — and updates if you change the unit while a dimension line is selected.
TipDimension lines are at their most useful over a plan drawn to a sensible scale — a room, a garden bed, a piece of furniture. Set the measurement unit to millimetres or centimetres first so the labels read in real-world terms.

Linking objects with connectors

A connector is a line that is anchored to two objects. Move or resize either object and the connector follows, staying attached — so a flow chart or a wiring diagram keeps its links intact however you rearrange it.

To join two objects with a connector

  1. Choose the Connector tool.
  2. Press on the first object, drag to the second, and release. Each end that lands on an object anchors to it.
  3. Now switch to the Select tool and drag either object — the connector stretches to keep them joined.
NoteAn end that is dropped on empty canvas stays a free point; an end dropped on an object anchors to that object’s centre. Connectors are saved with the drawing and exported into the SVG as real lines.
TipBuild a flow chart from a row of rectangles joined by connectors, then shuffle the boxes about to find the clearest layout — the connectors redraw themselves, so you never have to.
Chapter 16

Effects: Shadow and Glow

Two filter effects lift an object off the flat canvas: a drop shadow that casts it forward, and an outer glow that haloes it. Both are set in one dialog and can be used together.

Adding a drop shadow

To add a drop shadow

  1. Select the object with the Select tool.
  2. Click Effects… on the Style toolbar.
  3. Tick Enable drop shadow.
  4. Set the offset across and offset down (how far the shadow is thrown), the blur (how soft it is), the strength (how dark), and a colour.
  5. Click OK.

A soft shadow a little down and to the right is the classic way to make a shape look as if it floats a few millimetres above the page.

Adding an outer glow

To add an outer glow

  1. Select the object and open Effects….
  2. Tick Enable outer glow.
  3. Set the spread (how far the glow reaches) and the strength (how strong), and a colour.
  4. Click OK.

A glow in a bright, warm colour draws the eye to a highlight; a soft white glow lifts a shape off a dark background. An object can carry a shadow and a glow at the same time — tick both.

Removing an effect

To take an effect off again, open Effects… and untick the box for the shadow or the glow, then click OK. The effect is removed; the object itself is untouched.

Chapter 17

Layers and Arranging Objects

Every object sits in a stack, and newer objects cover older ones. Two tools control that stack: z-order commands that shuffle one object up or down, and layers that group objects so you can hide, reorder or re-home a whole set at once.

Stacking order (z-order)

When objects overlap, the one drawn later sits on top. The Arrange menu lets you change which is in front without redrawing anything.

To change the stacking order

  1. Select an object with the Select tool.
  2. Choose Arrange ▸ Bring to Front (Ctrl+Shift+]) or Send to Back (Ctrl+Shift+[) to jump it to the very top or bottom,
  3. or Bring Forward (Ctrl+]) / Send Backward (Ctrl+[) to move it one step at a time.

The Layers panel

For anything more than a few objects, layers keep a drawing organised. A layer is a named, show/hideable group; objects on a higher layer always sit above those on a lower one.

Open it from Arrange ▸ Show Layers Panel if it is closed. The panel lists layers with the front-most at the top; the row's tick shows or hides that layer.

To work with layers

  1. Click ＋ to add a new layer, or － to delete the current one (and everything on it).
  2. Use ▲ and ▼ to move the selected layer up or down the stack — which changes the paint order.
  3. Click ✎ to rename a layer; untick its box to hide it.
  4. New objects are drawn onto the currently selected layer. To move an existing object, select it, then pick a layer from the Selection → list.
NoteLayers are saved inside the SVG along with the drawing, so a reopened file keeps its exact layer stack, names and visibility. Older DRAWmaster files that pre-date layers still open perfectly — every object simply lands on a single default layer.
TipA common scheme: a Background layer for a filled rectangle or gradient, a middle layer for the main shapes, and a Text & labels layer on top — hide the text layer while you arrange the artwork, then show it again.
Chapter 18

Grouping, Aligning and Distributing

Once a drawing has more than a handful of objects you will want to handle several at once — pick out a set, lock them together as a group, and line them up tidily with the Align and Distribute commands.

Selecting more than one object

Every align, distribute and group command works on the current selection — so the first step is always to select the objects you mean.

To select several objects

  1. Choose the Select tool.
  2. Click the first object, then Shift-click each of the others to add it to the selection (Shift-click a selected one again to drop it).
  3. Or drag a rubber-band box across empty canvas — every object it touches is selected together.
NoteDragging any object in a multiple selection moves the whole set at once, keeping their relative positions. Pressing Delete removes them all.

Grouping objects

A group binds a set of objects into one. Click any member and the whole group selects; move, rotate or delete it and every member follows. It is the right tool for something built from several parts — a logo, a signpost, a little character — that you want to treat as a single thing from then on.

To group and ungroup

  1. Select two or more objects.
  2. Choose Arrange ▸ Group (Ctrl+G). They become one group.
  3. To break it apart again, select the group and choose Arrange ▸ Ungroup (Ctrl+Shift+G).
NoteGroups are saved inside the SVG with the drawing, so a reopened file keeps every group intact.

Aligning objects

The Align commands line selected objects up against a common edge or centre, worked out from the selection itself — so Align Left moves them all to the leftmost edge in the set, Align Middle centres them on a shared horizontal line, and so on.

To align a selection

  1. Select two or more objects.
  2. Open Arrange ▸ Align and choose Left, Centre or Right to line them up sideways,
  3. or Top, Middle or Bottom to line them up vertically.

Distributing objects

Where Align lines objects up, Distribute spaces them out evenly. Give it three or more objects and it keeps the two outermost where they are, then slides the ones between so the gaps are equal.

To distribute a selection

  1. Select three or more objects.
  2. Choose Arrange ▸ Distribute ▸ Horizontally to even out their left-to-right spacing,
  3. or Distribute ▸ Vertically to even out their top-to-bottom spacing.
TipAlign then distribute is the quickest way to tidy a row of buttons, a column of labels or a grid of icons: align them to a shared edge first, then distribute to space them evenly.
Chapter 19

Grid, Guides and Snapping

Precision work is far easier with something to line things up against. DRAWmaster offers a grid, draggable guides, and snapping that pulls objects neatly into place against the grid, the guides and each other. None of it prints — it is drawing scaffolding only.

Showing the grid

The grid is a faint mesh of lines across the canvas, a ruler you can see.

To show the grid and set its spacing

  1. Choose View ▸ Show Grid (Ctrl+') to switch it on or off.
  2. Choose View ▸ Grid Spacing… and type the gap between lines in pixels.
NoteThe grid is purely a guide for your eye and for snapping. It never appears in an exported PNG or SVG — the output shows only your artwork.

Adding guides

Guides are individual lines — one across, one down — that you place exactly where you want a shared edge or centre-line to be, then line objects up against.

To add and clear guides

  1. Choose View ▸ Add Horizontal Guide… or Add Vertical Guide….
  2. Type the position in pixels and click OK; a dashed guide line appears.
  3. Choose View ▸ Clear Guides to remove them all.

Snapping

With snapping on, an object you move or resize jumps the last few pixels to line up with the nearest grid line, guide, or the edge or centre of another object — so things sit flush without you having to be pixel-perfect by hand.

To use snapping

  1. Make sure View ▸ Snap to Grid & Guides is ticked (it is on by default).
  2. Switch on the grid, or add a guide or two, to give snapping something to catch on.
  3. Drag an object near a grid line, a guide or another object’s edge — it snaps into alignment as you release.
TipSnapping reads an object’s edges and its centre, and the same for its neighbours — so you can snap two shapes centre-to-centre, or butt one flush against another, as easily as snapping to the grid.
RememberIf a shape refuses to sit exactly where you drop it, that is snapping doing its job. Turn it off from View ▸ Snap to Grid & Guides for free-hand placement, then turn it back on.

Measurement units

The status bar and every dimension-line label can read out in pixels, millimetres or centimetres. The drawing itself is always stored in pixels — the unit only changes how lengths are shown, so switching units never moves or resizes anything.

To choose a measurement unit

  1. Open View ▸ Measurement Units.
  2. Choose Pixels, Millimetres or Centimetres.
  3. The pointer read-out in the status bar switches at once, and any selected dimension line re-labels itself in the new unit.
NoteDRAWmaster converts at 96 pixels to the inch (so 96 px = 25.4 mm = 2.54 cm) — the standard screen resolution, and the same convention its PDF export uses. For a drawing whose pixel size you have chosen to match a real sheet, the millimetre and centimetre read-outs are true to size.
TipWorking on a plan or a technical drawing? Switch to millimetres or centimetres before you add dimension lines, so every measured label reads in real-world units.
Chapter 20

Undo, Redo and Working Safely

Drawing is a process of trying things. DRAWmaster keeps a deep history of your changes, so you can experiment freely and step back whenever something does not work.

Undo and redo

Nearly everything you do — drawing a shape, moving it, recolouring it, adding an effect, deleting something — is recorded.

To step back and forward through your work

  1. Choose Edit ▸ Undo (Ctrl+Z) to reverse the last change.
  2. Keep pressing to walk back through the history, step by step.
  3. Choose Edit ▸ Redo (Ctrl+Shift+Z) to re-apply a change you undid.
NoteThe history holds many steps, so you can undo a whole run of changes — not just the most recent one. Starting a fresh change, though, clears the “redo” branch from that point on.

A safe way to work

Because Undo is deep and reliable, the best way to learn DRAWmaster is to try things. Draw a shape, recolour it, pile on a shadow and a glow, drag it about — and if you do not like the result, undo back to where you were. Save often (Ctrl+S) once a drawing is going well, so you always have a known-good version to return to.

Part III
Worked Projects
Chapter 21

Project: A Simple Logo

This project builds the badge-style logo you have seen in this guide, from an empty canvas to a finished mark — putting the skills of Part II to work in order: QuickShapes, fills and outlines, and effects.

Start with a backing shape

To lay the foundation

  1. Choose File ▸ New… and a square 800 × 800 canvas — logos suit a square.
  2. Pick a deep colour on the Fill button and a darker one on Line, with a wide Width.
  3. From the Shape list choose Octagon and drag out a large backing shape.
  4. Open Effects… and give it a soft drop shadow so it lifts off the page.

Add the central symbol

Now place the mark the logo is built around — here, a star.

To add the central symbol

  1. Set a bright Fill (a warm gold) and a matching Line.
  2. Choose the Star (5-point) QuickShape and drag it out, centred on the octagon.
  3. Open Effects… and add a gentle outer glow in a pale version of the fill, so the star seems to shine.

Finish with supporting shapes

A few supporting shapes round the logo out — a heart and a speech bubble here, each in its own colour.

To add the finishing shapes

  1. Draw a Heart QuickShape in a strong accent colour.
  2. Draw a Speech bubble with a white fill and a coloured outline.
  3. Nudge each into place with the Select tool until the arrangement feels balanced.

Export and reuse

With the logo finished, save it and export it for use elsewhere.

To save and export the logo

  1. Choose File ▸ Save as SVG… so you can re-open and edit it later.
  2. Choose File ▸ Export PNG… for a ready-to-use bitmap — to drop into a document, a website or an email.
TipKeep the SVG as your master. If the brand colour ever changes, re-open it, recolour the shapes and re-export — no quality is ever lost, because it is vector.
Chapter 22

Project: An Icon and a Diagram

Two more short projects show the range of a vector tool: a clean app-style icon, and a simple flow diagram built from shapes and arrows.

A clean icon

An icon is a logo stripped to its simplest: one strong shape, one clear symbol, no clutter.

To draw a flat icon

  1. Start from a square canvas.
  2. Draw a Rectangle that fills most of the canvas, with a bold fill and no outline (Width 0) — the rounded modern look.
  3. Draw one simple symbol on top — a QuickShape such as a Lightning bolt, Heart or Star — in white or a contrasting colour.
  4. Export a PNG at the size you need it.
RememberAn icon is read at a tiny size. Resist adding detail that will vanish when it is 32 pixels wide — one shape and one symbol is usually plenty.

A flow diagram

Vector shapes and arrows make a tidy diagram that you can always rearrange.

To build a flow diagram

  1. Draw a row of Rectangles (or ellipses) for the steps, all the same fill.
  2. Between each pair, draw an Arrow QuickShape, or a Line, pointing from one to the next.
  3. Use the Pen tool for a branch that bends around a corner.
  4. Keep the fills to two or three colours so the diagram reads calmly.
TipBecause every box and arrow is a separate object, you can drag a step to a new place and redraw just the arrows around it — far quicker than redrawing the whole diagram.
Part IV
Output & Sharing
Chapter 23

Exporting and Sharing

A finished drawing is meant to be used — on a web page, in a document, in an email, or touched up as a photo. DRAWmaster exports to the two formats that cover all of those.

Saving an editable SVG

SVG is DRAWmaster's own save format — a vector file that stays editable.

To save as SVG

  1. Choose File ▸ Save as SVG… (Ctrl+S).
  2. Name it and save. The drawing goes to your Documents/just a… folder by default.
NoteA DRAWmaster SVG is a genuine, standard SVG — a browser or another vector program will display it. DRAWmaster also tucks its full editable object list inside, so it can re-open the file with every shape intact. Edit a DRAWmaster SVG in another program and that editable copy may no longer match, so keep DRAWmaster’s SVG as your master.

Exporting a PNG

A PNG is a bitmap — the right format when you need a fixed-size picture to drop into a document, a website, a chat or an email, where SVG might not be accepted.

To export a PNG

  1. Choose File ▸ Export PNG….
  2. Name it and save. It is written at the canvas’s pixel size, on a white background, into your Pictures/just a… folder by default.
TipNeed the PNG bigger and still crisp? Start a larger canvas (or scale the whole drawing up) before exporting — because the drawing is vector, a larger export is just as sharp, unlike enlarging a PNG after the fact.

Touching up in PAINTcanvas

When a finished drawing needs raster-style work — a textured background, a photographic blend, a filter — DRAWmaster hands it to its sister app.

To edit a drawing in PAINTcanvas

  1. Choose File ▸ Edit in PAINTcanvas….
  2. DRAWmaster rasterises the drawing to a PNG and opens it in PAINTcanvas.
  3. Do your pixel-level work there and save.
RememberThis is a one-way trip: a drawing becomes a bitmap when it crosses to PAINTcanvas, and a bitmap cannot be broken back into editable vector shapes. Keep your SVG master so you can always go back to the editable version.
Chapter 24

Exporting to PDF and Printing

For a page you mean to print, hand over or archive, DRAWmaster writes a vector PDF — and can send the drawing straight to a printer. Both keep the artwork sharp: text stays text and shapes stay crisp paths, at any size.

Exporting a PDF

A PDF is the universal document format — it opens anywhere, prints faithfully, and (because DRAWmaster writes it as vector) stays razor-sharp however far it is zoomed or scaled.

To export a PDF

  1. Choose File ▸ Export PDF….
  2. Name the file and save. The PDF is written at the canvas size, into your Documents/just a… folder by default.
NoteThe PDF is painted through the same engine that draws the screen, so every shape, gradient, effect, image and piece of text appears exactly as it does on the canvas — and text is real, selectable text in the PDF, not a picture of letters.
TipA vector PDF is the right thing to send to a print shop or to drop into a report: it scales to any paper size without a hint of blur.

Printing

You can also print a drawing directly from DRAWmaster.

To print a drawing

  1. Choose File ▸ Print… (Ctrl+P).
  2. Pick your printer and page options in the print dialog.
  3. Click Print. The drawing is scaled to fit the page and printed as sharp vector artwork.
RememberThe drawing is sized to fit the selected paper while keeping its proportions — so a wide canvas prints landscape-wide on the page, with a margin above and below. Choose a matching paper orientation for the fullest use of the sheet.

Chapter 28

Appendix D — Glossary

The drawing words used in this guide.

A–Z

Alpha
The opacity of a colour — a low alpha makes a fill partly see-through.
Arrowhead
A filled triangle placed at the start or end of a line or path, for pointers and connectors.
Bézier curve
A smooth curve defined by nodes and their control handles — the mathematics behind every vector curve.
Bitmap (raster)
A picture made of a grid of coloured dots, such as a PNG or a photo; it blurs when enlarged.
Combine (boolean)
Weld two or more shapes into one with Union, Subtract or Intersect.
Connector
A line anchored to two objects that stays attached as they move or resize.
Dimension line
A measured line with end ticks and an automatic length label, for plans and diagrams.
Duplicate (clone)
An offset copy of the selection, made with Ctrl+D.
Flip
Mirror an object left-to-right or top-to-bottom about the selection’s centre.
Lock
Pin an object so it cannot be selected or moved by accident, until unlocked.
Measurement unit
Pixels, millimetres or centimetres — how lengths are shown; the drawing itself stays in pixels.
Texture (pattern) fill
A fill that paints a tiled or stretched image inside a shape.
Text on a path
Artistic text flowed along a line or curve so its letters follow the path.
Control handle
A small marker on a stalk from a node that steers how a Bézier curve bends through it.
Convert to Curves
Turn a shape, line or QuickShape into an editable node path.
Dash style
Whether a line is drawn solid, dashed or dotted.
Image
A bitmap picture placed on the canvas as an object and embedded in the drawing.
Node
A point on a path; corner nodes turn sharply, smooth nodes curve gracefully.
Opacity
How solid an object is, from transparent to fully opaque; lower lets what is behind show through.
PDF
A universal document format; DRAWmaster exports a vector PDF that stays sharp at any size.
Drop shadow
A soft, offset copy behind an object that makes it look raised off the page.
Align
Line selected objects up against a shared edge or centre.
Distribute
Space three or more selected objects evenly between the outermost two.
Fill
The colour inside a shape.
Freehand
A path drawn by hand, following the pointer like a pencil.
Grid
A faint, non-printing mesh of lines across the canvas, for lining things up and for snapping.
Group
Several objects bound into one, so they select, move, rotate and delete together.
Guide
A single non-printing line, across or down, placed to line objects up against.
Handle
A small marker on a selected object’s frame — eight square resize handles and one round rotate handle.
Gradient
A fill that blends smoothly between two colours — linear (across the shape) or radial (out from the centre).
Layer
A named, show/hideable group of objects; higher layers sit above lower ones in the drawing.
Object
Anything you draw — a shape, a line, a path or text; each is selected and styled on its own.
Outer glow
A soft halo of colour around an object.
Outline (line / stroke)
The coloured edge around a shape, or the body of a line.
Path
A freehand stroke, stored as the series of points it followed.
Pen / polyline
A shape built point by point; closed and filled, or left as an open line.
PNG
A common bitmap image format; DRAWmaster exports to it for fixed-size pictures.
QuickShape
A ready-made shape outline (star, arrow, heart, speech bubble…).
Rotate
Turn an object about its centre; the angle is stored and exported as an SVG transform.
Snapping
Pulling a moved or resized object into line with the grid, a guide or another object.
Transform
A change to an object’s size or angle — resizing or rotating.
SVG
Scalable Vector Graphics — DRAWmaster’s editable save format, and a web standard.
Text (artistic text)
Words as a drawing object — fillable, outlinable, gradient-fillable, and exported as real SVG text.
Vector
Artwork defined by maths, not pixels — sharp at any size.
Z-order
The front-to-back stacking of overlapping objects; set with the Arrange commands.
Width
The thickness of an outline, in pixels; 0 means no outline.
Chapter 29

Appendix E — DrawPlus X3 Cross-Reference

DRAWmaster is a clean-room drawing program in the tradition of Serif's DrawPlus X3. This appendix walks the thirteen chapters of the DrawPlus X3 User Guide in order and says, honestly, where DRAWmaster does the same thing, where it does something close, and where a DrawPlus feature is deliberately not part of this edition — so you have a complete map between the two.

How to read this appendix

Each section below corresponds to a DrawPlus X3 chapter. A table lists that chapter's main topics with one of three verdicts:

  • In DRAWmaster — DRAWmaster has the same (or an equivalent) feature; the “where” column points to the chapter of this guide that covers it.
  • Partly — DRAWmaster does something close but not identical.
  • Not in this edition — a DrawPlus feature this edition does not replicate, listed so the map is complete.
NoteDRAWmaster is a focused vector editor, not a full DrawPlus clone. The honest “Not in this edition” notes below are the features that make DrawPlus a much larger program — animation, pressure brushes, autotrace, 3D and the distortion tools — and are the natural places it could grow.

Chapter 30

Appendix F — Troubleshooting

Quick answers to common snags.

Common questions

My shape has no outline.
The Width is set to 0, or the Line colour is unset. Raise the width and pick a line colour on the Style toolbar.
My shape has no fill — it is hollow.
Lines and open pen paths never fill. For a shape, click the Fill button and pick a colour; a filled object draws solid.
I can’t select the object I want.
Clicking picks the topmost object. Move the one on top aside, or delete it, to reach what is behind.
My pen shape won’t fill.
You pressed Enter, which finishes an open line. Finish with a double-click to close and fill the shape instead.
I opened an SVG and couldn’t edit its shapes.
That SVG was made by another program. DRAWmaster can re-open with full editing only the SVGs it saved itself.
My effect vanished when I exported a PNG.
It should not — shadows and glows are drawn into the export. If a glow looks faint, raise its strength, then export again.
